before: Under the Medicare Secondary Payer Act (42 U.S.C. § 1395y(b)), Medicare must be repaid from any liability settlement, judgment or award, whether or not it mentions medical expenses. This federal right overrides state lien and made-whole rules and can be reduced, waived or compromised only through Medicare's own procedures; CMS does not pursue physical-trauma liability settlements of $750 or less.

This federal right overrides state lien and made-whole rules and can be reduced, waived or compromised only through Medicare's own procedures; CMS does not pursue physical-trauma liability settlements of $750 or less. Medicare Advantage plans assert the same secondary-payer recovery rights (42 C.F.R. § 422.108).

after: However, in Arkansas Dept. of Health & Human Services v. Ahlborn (2006), the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that Medicaid can only assert a lien against the portion of a settlement representing medical expenses — not the entire recovery. This ruling provides a basis for reducing Medicaid liens, especially when non-medical damages like pain and suffering make up the bulk of the settlement. Later decisions refined the rule: a state cannot simply presume that a fixed share of the recovery is medical (Wos v. E.M.A., 2013), but it may recover from the portion allocated to future as well as past medical care (Gallardo v. Marstiller, 2022).
